statement: About a given circle to circumscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon.
heath_proof: Let ABCDE be the given circle; thus it is required to circumscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon about the circle ABCDE. Let A, B, C, D, E be conceived to be the angular points of the inscribed pentagon, so that the circumferences AB, BC, CD, DE, EA are equal; [IV. 11] through A, B, C, D, E let GH, HK, KL, LM, MG be drawn touching the circle; [III. 16] let the centre F of the circle ABCDE be taken [III. 1], and let FB, FK, FC, FL, FD be joined. Then, since the straight line KL touches the circle ABCDE at C, and FC has been joined from the centre F to the point of contact at C, therefore FC is perpendicular to KL; [III. 18] therefore each of the angles at C is right. For the same reason the angles at the points B, D are also right. And, since the angle FCK is right, therefore the square on FK is equal to the squares on FC, CK. For the same reason [I. 47] the square on FK is also equal to the squares on FB, BK; so that the squares on FC, CK are equal to the squares on FB, BK, of which the square on FC is equal to the square on FB; therefore the square on CK which remains is equal to the square on BK. Therefore BK is equal to CK. And, since FB is equal to FC, and FK common, the two sides BF, FK are equal to the two sides CF, FK; and the base BK equal to the base CK; therefore the angle BFK is equal to the angle KFC, [I. 8]and the angle BKF to the angle FKC. Therefore the angle BFC is double of the angle KFC, and the angle BKC of the angle FKC. For the same reason the angle CFD is also double of the angle CFL, and the angle DLC of the angle FLC. Now, since the circumference BC is equal to CD, the angle BFC is also equal to the angle CFD. [III. 27] And the angle BFC is double of the angle KFC, and the angle DFC of the angle LFC; therefore the angle KFC is also equal to the angle LFC. But the angle FCK is also equal to the angle FCL; therefore FKC, FLC are two triangles having two angles equal to two angles and one side equal to one side, namely FC which is common to them; therefore they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides, and the remaining angle to the remaining angle; [I. 26] therefore the straight line KC is equal to CL, and the angle FKC to the angle FLC. And, since KC is equal to CL, therefore KL is double of KC. For the same reason it can be proved that HK is also double of BK.  And BK is equal to KC; therefore HK is also equal to KL. Similarly each of the straight lines HG, GM, ML can also be proved equal to each of the straight lines HK, KL; therefore the pentagon GHKLM is equilateral. I say next that it is also equiangular. For, since the angle FKC is equal to the angle FLC, and the angle HKL was proved double of the angle FKC, and the angle KLM double of the angle FLC, therefore the angle HKL is also equal to the angle KLM. Similarly each of the angles KHG, HGM, GML can also be proved equal to each of the angles HKL, KLM; therefore the five angles GHK, HKL, KLM, LMG, MGH are equal to one another. Therefore the pentagon GHKLM is equiangular. And it was also proved equilateral; and it has been circumscribed about the circle ABCDE.

4.12
**Statement:** About a given circle to circumscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon.

**Step 1.** Let the given circle have center O. By 4.11, inscribe in it an equilateral and equiangular pentagon ABCDE, so that arcs AB, BC, CD, DE, and EA are all equal.

**Step 2.** By 3.30, bisect each of the arcs AB, BC, CD, DE, EA at points F, G, H, K, L respectively. Then arc AF = arc FB, arc BG = arc GC, arc CH = arc HD, arc DK = arc KE, and arc EL = arc LA.

**Step 3.** At each of the points F, G, H, K, L, draw the straight line perpendicular to the radius at that point (by 1.11 and 1.12 of the construction, or directly by 3.16, which establishes that the line at right angles to a diameter at its extremity touches the circle). By 3.16, each such line is tangent to the circle at that point. Thus each side of the circumscribed figure touches the circle, as required by D4.4.

**Step 4.** Let the tangent at F and the tangent at G meet at point M; let the tangent at G and the tangent at H meet at N; let the tangent at H and the tangent at K meet at P; let the tangent at K and the tangent at L meet at Q; and let the tangent at L and the tangent at F meet at R. Then MNPQR is a pentagon circumscribed about the circle.

**Step 5.** Since arc AF = arc FB and arc BG = arc GC, and arc AB = arc BC (the inscribed pentagon being equilateral, so by 3.26 its equal chords subtend equal arcs), we have arc FG = arc FB + arc BG = (1/2) arc AB + (1/2) arc BC = (1/2)(arc AB + arc BC) = arc AB. Similarly, arc GH = arc HC + arc CD/2 + ... more precisely: arc GH = arc GC + arc CH = (1/2) arc BC + (1/2) arc CD = (1/2)(arc BC + arc CD) = arc BC = arc AB. By the same reasoning, arcs HK, KL, and LF each equal arc AB. Therefore arcs FG, GH, HK, KL, and LF are all equal to one another.

**Step 6.** Since arcs FG, GH, HK, KL, LF are equal, by 3.27 the angles they subtend at the center O are equal. That is, angle FOG = angle GOH = angle HOK = angle KOL = angle LOF. Since these five equal angles together make up the full angle about O (four right angles), each equals four-fifths of a right angle.

**Step 7.** Consider point M where the tangents at F and G meet. By 3.18, since the tangent at F touches the circle at F, the line OF is perpendicular to the tangent at F, so angle OFM is a right angle. Similarly, angle OGM is a right angle. In the quadrilateral OFMG, the angle sum equals four right angles (by 1.32 applied to the two triangles formed by diagonal OM). Since angle OFM and angle OGM are each right angles and angle FOG = four-fifths of a right angle, we have angle FMG = 4 right angles - right angle - right angle - (4/5 right angle) = (2 - 4/5) right angles = 6/5 right angles.

**Step 8.** By the identical argument at each vertex: in quadrilateral OGNH, angle GNH = 4 right angles - right angle - right angle - angle GOH = 6/5 right angles. Similarly angle HPK = angle KQL = angle LRF = 6/5 right angles. Therefore all five angles of pentagon MNPQR are equal.

**Step 9.** Now consider the two right triangles OFM and OGM. We have OF = OG (radii of the same circle), angle OFM = angle OGM = right angle, and OM is common. Since the angle FOM = angle GOM (each being half of angle FOG, as follows: triangles OFM and OGM have OF = OG, OM common, and angle OFM = angle OGM, so by subtracting the squares on the equal sides OF, OG from the square on the common hypotenuse OM using 1.47, we get FM = GM; then by 1.8, triangles OFM and OGM are congruent, giving angle FOM = angle GOM). Therefore FM = GM.

**Step 10.** By the same argument at point N: in right triangles OGN and OHN, OG = OH (radii), angle OGN = angle OHN = right angle, ON is common, so GN = HN. At point P: HP = KP. At point Q: KQ = LQ. At point R: LR = FR.

**Step 11.** Furthermore, since angle FOM = (1/2) angle FOG = (2/5) right angle, and angle GON = (1/2) angle GOH = (2/5) right angle, the right triangles OGM and OGN have: OG is common, angle OGM = angle OGN = right angle, and angle GOM = angle GON = (2/5) right angle. Therefore by 1.26 (AAS), triangle OGM is congruent to triangle OGN, and hence GM = GN.

**Step 12.** By the same reasoning applied at each tangent point: at H, using triangles OHN and OHP (with angle HON = angle HOP = 2/5 right angle), we get HN = HP. At K: KP = KQ. At L: LQ = LR. At F: FR = FM.

**Step 13.** Now side MN of the pentagon equals MG + GN (since G lies on segment MN, being the point of tangency on that side). We have MG = GM and GN from above. Similarly, side NP = NH + HP, side PQ = PK + KQ, side QR = QL + LR, side RM = RF + FM.

**Step 14.** From Step 9, FM = GM. From Step 11, GM = GN. Therefore FM = GM = GN. By the analogous results at each tangent point (Steps 10 and 12): GN = HN = HP = KP = KQ = LQ = LR = FR = FM. All these tangent half-segments are equal.

**Step 15.** Therefore MN = MG + GN = 2·GM, and NP = NH + HP = 2·HN = 2·GM, and PQ = PK + KQ = 2·KP = 2·GM, and QR = QL + LR = 2·LQ = 2·GM, and RM = RF + FM = 2·FM = 2·GM. By CN1, all five sides are equal, so the pentagon MNPQR is equilateral.

**Step 16.** Since all five angles of MNPQR are equal (Step 8) and all five sides are equal (Step 15), the pentagon MNPQR is both equilateral and equiangular. Each side touches the given circle (Step 3), so by D4.4, the pentagon is circumscribed about the given circle.

**Step 17.** Therefore, about the given circle an equilateral and equiangular pentagon has been circumscribed, which is what was required to do.
